actions.justification: Mandatory first step - the Pediatric Assessment Triangle (appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin) provides rapid initial assessment of illness severity in pediatric patients.
Mandatory - age-appropriate vital sign assessment is critical in pediatric patients, especially with congenital heart disease, as normal ranges differ by age.
Mandatory - accurate weight in kg is essential for weight-based dosing of all medications in pediatric patients.

Mandatory action - must be completed within 60 minutes. Establishing vascular access is critical for any potential medication administration or fluid resuscitation in this patient with congenital heart disease.
Assessing mental status is an important secondary evaluation to identify any neurological compromise or altered consciousness in this pediatric patient with congenital heart disease.
Point-of-care glucose check is indicated in pediatric patients, especially those with congenital heart disease, to rule out hypoglycemia as a contributing factor to their presentation.

Mandatory action: Administer NS bolus at 20ml/kg as per fluid resuscitation protocol. Patient has IV access established. Use caution given congenital heart disease - administer slowly and reassess frequently.
Mandatory action: Monitor urine output to assess fluid responsiveness and end-organ perfusion, especially important in a patient with congenital heart disease who may be sensitive to fluid overload.
Mandatory action: Reassess patient after each fluid bolus to evaluate response and watch for signs of fluid overload or hemodynamic deterioration, critical in congenital heart disease.
Calculate Broselow weight to ensure accurate weight-based dosing for any medications that may be needed, especially important in pediatric patients with congenital heart disease.
Administer H1 antihistamine as part of allergic/anaphylactic reaction management protocol if this is an allergic presentation, weight-based dosing appropriate for pediatric patient.

Administer corticosteroid weight-based to reduce inflammation and secondary reaction, appropriate secondary treatment in allergic or inflammatory conditions, especially in a child with congenital heart disease.
Ensure reliable IV access is in place for medication administration and fluid delivery, especially given congenital heart disease history requiring careful hemodynamic management.
Supplemental oxygen is appropriate supportive care, particularly in a patient with congenital heart disease to optimize oxygen delivery.
Patient has congenital heart disease; cautious fluid support may be needed. Monitor response closely given cardiac comorbidity.

Patient with congenital heart disease requires close monitoring after interventions; vitals are currently stable but ongoing assessment is critical given underlying cardiac comorbidity and pending labs.
Respiratory monitoring is essential in a patient with congenital heart disease who has received fluid boluses and antihistamines; SpO2 is currently 98% but can deteriorate rapidly in this population.
Patient with congenital heart disease and ongoing treatment may require rapid medication or fluid administration; a second IV access provides redundancy and faster delivery capacity.
CBC to evaluate for infection, anemia, or other hematologic abnormalities relevant to this patient with congenital heart disease and pending workup.
BMP to assess electrolytes, renal function, and glucose in this patient with congenital heart disease who has received fluid boluses.
Blood gas to assess oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status in a patient with congenital heart disease to ensure adequate cardiopulmonary function.
Patient with congenital heart disease and prior fluid boluses warrants lactate measurement to assess perfusion adequacy and detect occult hypoperfusion/shock despite currently stable vitals.

Patient has received antihistamines, corticosteroids, and fluid boluses suggesting anaphylaxis/allergic reaction management. With congenital heart disease, airway protection should be proactively assessed especially if angioedema or respiratory compromise could develop.

If this is anaphylaxis (suggested by prior H1 antihistamine and corticosteroid administration), epinephrine IM is the first-line treatment. With congenital heart disease, anaphylaxis carries higher risk and epinephrine should be given if not already administered or if symptoms persist/recur.
